agent_notes: עֲרָבִים: 'poplars' (Populus euphratica, the Euphrates poplar) rather than KJV 'willows'. I rely on Rashi and Metzudat Zion for the link to עַרְבֵי־נַחַל (Lev 23:40) and on BDB for the botanical identification; the tree species is the standard modern view, not stated in the packet.

תוֹלָלֵינוּ is a hapax and the commentators split three ways. (1) Instruments that are 'hung': Rashi's first reading (after Menahem), Ibn Ezra (at v. 2: 'ותוללינו ותליתינו כלי השמחה') and Radak, who paraphrases the verse as 'they asked us to rejoice with our lyres that we hung on the poplars'. (2) 'Our mockers' from הלל: Rashi's second reading (citing Ps 102:9), Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion. (3) 'Our wailing' from ילל: Meiri, and the 'some interpret' that Radak cites (Moses ha-Kohen, whom Ibn Ezra rejects, per the reviewer's request). I render 'those who mock us' because it parallels 'our captors' and matches the STEPBible gloss; the other readings are in the note. The verb 'asked' is shared by both halves, so '[asked]' is bracketed.

(PS.137.3 Radak: "ובכינורותינו שתלינו על הערבים היו שואלים אותנו שנשמח בהם, ויש מפרשים תוללינו כמו יללתינו"; Ibn Ezra (at PS.137.2): "והנה ותוללינו ותליתינו כלי השמחה")

agent_notes: אֵיךְ is the short form of אֵיכָה (Lam 1:1), as the reviewer asked; I state it in the commentary and the note. 'Ground of a foreign god' is the reading of Ibn Ezra and Radak, who take נֵכָר as short for אֵל נֵכָר.

agent_notes: The second clause has no 'her cunning' in the Hebrew: תִּשְׁכַּח יְמִינִי has no object. KJV and ASV supply 'cunning/skill'. I leave it unsupplied in the literal layer and put 'forget [its skill]' only as a bracketed option in the dramatic layer. Ibn Ezra notes the omission ('חסר כמו המעשה').

אַעֲלֶה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַם עַל רֹאשׁ שִׂמְחָתִי: 'lift up' is the literal verb; 'prefer' (KJV) is an interpretation. Rashi reads it as raising the memory of the destruction at the head of every joy (citing Bava Batra 60b); Metzudat David as 'at the beginning of joy'. The last sentence of the commentary now follows the reviewer: Meiri's apology reading (vv. 5-6 as the Levite's excuse that he sang under compulsion, not from the heart) and Radak's note that the Levites' words end here and vv. 7-9 are the psalmist's.

agent_notes: השְּׁדוּדָה is a passive participle ('the devastated one') used as a prophetic perfect or as 'about to be devastated'. STEPBible and KJV give a future sense; Malbim says Babylon had already been plundered by Cyrus. I render 'the devastated one' in the literal layer and flag both readings in the commentary.

The verse is rendered without softening ('smash', 'infants'). עוֹלָלַיִךְ is 'your nursing children / little ones' (Metzudat Zion cites Ps 8:3); KJV 'little ones' and 'stones' both soften (the Hebrew has singular 'the rock'). The commentary explains the imprecatory genre and the lex talionis reading without endorsing the act; Meiri ties it to Isa 13:16-18 and Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as repayment in kind.
Синодальный даёт «на вербах»; в комментарии и примечании к עֲרָבִים теперь так и цитируется. В буквальном слое оставлен «тополь», как в иврите-английском глоссе (евфратский тополь).

agent_notes: הַשְּׁדוּדָה: Синодальный перевод — «опустошительница» (активный смысл), еврейское причастие страдательное («опустошённая», «обречённая на разорение»); в переводе сохранён страдательный залог, расхождение с Синодальным отмечено в комментарии.
